title: Packing-first-fit vs Preemptive-fallback: runs and tradeoffs for heterogeneous inference adapters
content:
Purpose
This doc records a set of small-scale experiments comparing two runtime strategies for mixed backends (Triton/TensorRT/custom kernels):
  1) packing-first-fit scheduler: try to pack incoming requests into existing GPU execution slots (bins) and only start a fallback kernel instance if no suitable packing exists;
  2) preemptive-fallback scheduler: proactively route medium-latency requests to a cheaper slower kernel (e.g., quantized custom op) while reserving high-perf kernels for latency-critical requests, with the ability to preempt and migrate work when load changes.

Motivation and context
We are juggling three integration axes: (A) TensorRT-optimized inference for throughput/latency, (B) Triton as the model server surface with multi-instance and model control, (C) custom CUDA kernels for specialized op paths (quantized matmuls, grouped attention). Our production workloads have a mix of short streams (interactive chat) and long generations (batch/rescore). The key questions:
  - How to maximize GPU utilization without amplifying tail latency?
  - How does KV cache memory pressure interact with packing strategies?
  - When is it better to instantiate a fast but memory-hungry TRT instance vs reusing an existing custom-kernel slot?

Experiment setup (short)
- Hardware: 8x A100-40GB (shared cluster), tests pinned to single GPU for reproducible profiles and multi-GPU for cluster-level runs.
- Models: rw-6b (FP16), rw-13b-ql (quantized custom kernel), gpt-like small synthetic LM for microbenchmarks.
- Runtimes: TensorRT engine built from huggingface export, Triton 23.08 with model-repository multi-model instance config, custom kernel shim compiled into runtime.
- Workloads: 3 request mixes: 
  A) 80% short (<=128 tokens), 20% long (>=1024 tokens) streaming;
  B) 50/50;
  C) bursty arrival pattern (Poisson bursts) to stress preemption.
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p99 latency per-token and end-to-end, GPU memory occupancy, CUDA context switch counts, KV cache hit/evict counts, stalls due to kernel load, throughput (tokens/s).

Key findings (high-level)
1) Packing-first-fit wins on steady-state throughput for homogeneous short work: by tightly bin-packing short requests into existing decode threads we improved tokens/s by 12–18% over baseline Triton instance-per-model configuration. Latency p50 slightly improved; p99 slightly worsened under heavy load because long queued requests were sometimes delayed by aggressive packing.
2) Preemptive-fallback reduces p99 for mixed workloads: moving medium-priority requests to a quantized/custom path avoided saturating TRT instances and reduced p99 by up to 28% in the mixed (50/50) scenario. Cost was reduced tokens/s (5–10%) because quantized kernels had lower per-op parallelism and occasionally serialized work.
3) KV cache interaction is critical: packing-first-fit increased peak KV cache residency and fragmentation. We saw a higher KV eviction rate (approx +35%) when packing was aggressive because more independent streams were resident simultaneously, pushing cache pressure. This caused increased recompute of past tokens on long generations and raised effective latency for those streams.
4) Preemption overhead is non-trivial: migrating a stream from quantized custom kernel to TRT involved copying small-but-nonzero KV-state and warming the TRT KV cache; measured migration penalty ~12–40ms depending on cache size and seq-length. If preemption is frequent, these penalties accumulate and cancel p99 improvements.

Detailed experiment notes and traces
- Packing-first-fit behavior trace (short workload burst):
  * At T0 we packed 5 short streams into a single TRT decode slot (concurrent batches merged). GPU occupancy: 78% -> 94% during active decode; average batched sequence length increased from 40->63 tokens. Peak mem 28GB (headroom 12GB).
  * KV cache: 5 separate caches referenced, total KV bytes consumed ~3.4GB; fragmentation noted when streams ended at different times. Evictions started after sustained burst > 90s.
  * Observation: when a long generation arrived during packing, it either waited behind packed slots (p99 spike) or forced a fallback kernel to be launched (costly).
- Preemptive-fallback trace (mixed workload):
  * Metric gating: requests tagged by SLO label (low/med/high). Low/med mapped to quantized custom kernel; high to TRT. Under load, med streams were kept on custom path.
  * When burst subsided, we migrated some med streams onto TRT for quality reasons; migration involved copying KV rows (64kB typical) and running a one-shot warmup token. Total migration time distribution: median 18ms, 90th 38ms.
  * Observed a reduction of TRT queueing delays for high-SLO requests; overall cluster tokens/s dropped about 7% as custom kernels had lower FMA throughput on tested kernels.

Tradeoffs summary
- Packing-first-fit: +higher throughput, +better GPU utilization, -higher KV eviction and p99 for heterogeneous request lengths, + simpler runtime (less migration logic).
- Preemptive-fallback: +lower p99 under mixed loads, +explicit SLO control, -migration cost and added scheduling complexity, -lower aggregate throughput in our quantized custom kernels baseline.

Recommendations and practical configurations
1) Hybrid policy (recommended initial): use packing-first-fit as default for short-only or steady workloads. Enable preemptive-fallback only when request SLO profile indicates heavy tail and large variance.
2) KV-cache-aware packing: add a heuristic to estimate incremental KV footprint before packing a new stream into a slot. If estimated KV util pushes slot beyond a threshold (e.g., 70% of kernel KV reservation), refuse packing and prefer launching a fallback.
3) Migration budget: only allow migrations when expected migration cost < margin (SLO slack). Expose migration-cost telemetry and integrate into routing decision.
4) Warm TRTs with small prefix when preempting: to reduce migration penalty, perform a tiny warmup (1–4 tokens) in background so subsequent user-visible latency is smaller. Account for the warmup in cost model.
5) Experiment with hybrid kernels: identify hot op sequences that can run on custom kernels with similar throughput to TRT (fused attention + linear blocks). That can reduce the throughput gap we observed.

Open questions and next steps
- Can we reduce KV migration cost by storing compact delta encodings or shared on-device cache regions across kernel types?
- How does first-fit packing interact with multi-GPU shared KV (in Dedicated clusters)? Run cross-GPU eviction stress tests.
- Bench: run long-duration (24h) mixed workload to observe steady-state eviction cascades and rare failure modes.
- Engineering: prototype the KV-aware packing heuristic in the scheduler (RFC in GH PR #789). Also add a migration-cost estimator API to the runtime.

Quick TODOs
- [ ] Add KV-size estimate to request metadata (agent work).
- [ ] Implement simulated migration-cost calculator (Rahul).
- [ ] Run A/B with hybrid policy on staging cluster for 48h (Marco / SRE).
- [ ] Spike on shared KV region prototype (Elena).

Appendix: commands and minimal repro notes
- Build TRT engine: tools/export_to_trt.sh --model rw-6b --fp16 --opt_batch 8
- Triton launch (test config): tritonserver --model-repository /tmp/models --instance-gpus 0,1 --strict-model-config=false
- Custom kernel test harness: tools/run_custom_kernel_bench.py --kernel fused_attn_linear --batch 8 --seq 64 --it 2000
- Logging flags to enable: RUNTIME_SCHED_DEBUG=1, KV_TRACE=1, MIGRATION_SIM=1
